newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Lawyer says Argentina negotiated to allow in Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says Argentina negotiated to allow in Nazis.

text.p: A lawyer for a former SS officer facing a war crimes trial has said Argentina gave 2,000 blank passports and 8,000 other identification papers to Nazis who fled Germany at the end of the Second World War, the private DyN news agency reported on Sunday.
The agency quoted Pedro Bianchi as telling local media near his home in Bariloche that he worked as a lawyer in the Foreign Ministry from 1945 to 1947.
Neither Bianchi nor government officials could be reached for comment on Sunday to confirm the report, and Dyn did not identify the media source of the report.
DyN said former President Juan Domingo Peron, founder of the Peronist movement, had decided to give refuge to Nazis.

"In 1945 the government negotiated the supply of documentation to Germany that allowed the entry of Nazis in the country," Bianchi was quoted as saying, estimating that "about 2,000 blank passports and 8,000 identification papers of the same condition were distributed."
"Under this scheme only about 2,000 Nazis entered Argentina, many received the identification papers but they settled down in other countries such as Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay."

Bianchi has been a lawyer to Erich Priebke, accused of complicity in multiple murders for his acknowledged participation in the Ardeatine Caves massacre south of Rome in March 1944, when 335 men and boys were shot to death in reprisal for a partisan bomb attack.

Priebke, 83, has faced a military court in Rome but the trial, dogged by legal challenges, ended in uproar in August when the court found him guilty but ruled he was no longer liable for punishment. The verdict was later overturned and a new trial ordered.
Priebke was extradited more than a year ago from Argentina where he had lived since the end of the war.

Under Peron, an admirer of Italian fascist ruler Benito Mussolini, Argentina became a haven for war criminals such as Hilter confidante Martin Bormann, Auschwitz doctor Josef Mengele and Holocaust architect Adolf Eichmann.

A secret U.S. document declassified two months ago, sent from the U.S. Embassy in Buenos Aires in April 1945, estimated the Nazis secretly sent more than $1 billion for investment in Argentina just a month before the Second World War ended.
